claim: Four types (type I-IV) of eFOV-microendoscopes of various length and cross section were designed, all composed of a GRIN rod, a glass coverslip and a microfabricated corrective aspheric lens.
source: Four types (type I-IV) of eFOV-microendoscopes of various length and cross section were designed, all composed of a GRIN rod, a glass coverslip and a microfabricated corrective aspheric lens (Figure 1).

claim: eFOV-microendoscopes have lateral diameter between 0.35–0.5 mm.
source: GRIN rods and corrective lenses were different in each of the four types of eFOV-microendoscopes (lateral diameter, 0.35–0.5 mm; length, 1.1–4.1 mm; all 0.5 NA).
evidence: The text explicitly states the lateral diameter range of the eFOV-microendoscopes.

claim: eFOV-microendoscopes have length between 1.1–4.1 mm.
source: GRIN rods and corrective lenses were different in each of the four types of eFOV-microendoscopes (lateral diameter, 0.35–0.5 mm; length, 1.1–4.1 mm; all 0.5 NA).
evidence: The text explicitly states the length range of the eFOV-microendoscopes.

claim: All eFOV-microendoscopes have 0.5 NA.

evidence: The text explicitly states that all four types have 0.5 NA.

claim: The glass coverslip was 100 µm thick for type I, III, IV eFOV-microendoscopes.
source: The glass coverslip was 100 µm thick for type I, III, IV eFOV-microendoscopes and 200 µm thick for type II eFOV-microendoscopes.
evidence: The text explicitly states the coverslip thickness for types I, III, and IV.

claim: The glass coverslip was 200 µm thick for type II eFOV-microendoscopes.
source: The glass coverslip was 100 µm thick for type I, III, IV eFOV-microendoscopes and 200 µm thick for type II eFOV-microendoscopes.
evidence: The text explicitly states the coverslip thickness for type II.

claim: The eFOV-microendoscope design did not require additional cannulas or clamping devices.
source: This design did not require additional cannulas or clamping devices (Kim et al., 2012; Jung et al., 2004) that would increase the lateral size of the microendoscope assembly or reduce its usable length, respectively.
evidence: The text explicitly states that the design does not require additional cannulas or clamping devices, with citations to prior work that used such devices.

claim: Ray-trace simulations were performed at λ = 920 nm for each type of GRIN rod used in the eFOV-microendoscopes.
source: For each type of GRIN rod used in the eFOV-microendoscopes, ray-trace simulations were performed at λ = 920 nm and determined the profile of the aspheric lens (Figure 1) that corrected optical aberrations and maximized the FOV (Figure 2).
evidence: The text explicitly states that ray-trace simulations were performed at 920 nm wavelength, with results shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: For type I eFOV-microendoscopes, the simulated corrective lens had a diameter of 0.5 mm.
source: In the representative case of type I eFOV-microendoscopes, the simulated corrective lens had a diameter of 0.5 mm, height <40 µm, and the coefficients used in Equation (1) (see Materials and methods) to define the lens profile are reported in Supplementary file 1 - Table 1.
evidence: The text explicitly states the diameter of the simulated corrective lens for type I microendoscopes.

claim: For type I eFOV-microendoscopes, the simulated corrective lens had height <40 µm.
source: In the representative case of type I eFOV-microendoscopes, the simulated corrective lens had a diameter of 0.5 mm, height <40 µm, and the coefficients used in Equation (1) (see Materials and methods) to define the lens profile are reported in Supplementary file 1 - Table 1.
evidence: The text explicitly states the height of the simulated corrective lens for type I microendoscopes.

claim: For type I eFOV-microendoscopes, the Strehl ratio of the system was >80% at a distance up to ~165 µm from the optical axis with the corrective lens.
source: For this type of eFOV-microendoscope, the simulated point-spread-function (PSF) at incremental radial distances from the optical axis (up to 200 μm) showed that the Strehl ratio of the system was >80% (i.e. a diffraction-limited condition is achieved according to the Maréchal criterion [Smith, 2008]) at a distance up to ~165 µm from the optical axis with the corrective lens, while only up to ~70 µm for the same optical system without the corrective lens (Figure 2a).
evidence: The text explicitly states the Strehl ratio performance with the corrective lens, referencing Figure 2a and citing the Maréchal criterion.

claim: For type I eFOV-microendoscopes without the corrective lens, the Strehl ratio of the system was >80% only up to ~70 µm from the optical axis.
source: For this type of eFOV-microendoscope, the simulated point-spread-function (PSF) at incremental radial distances from the optical axis (up to 200 μm) showed that the Strehl ratio of the system was >80% (i.e. a diffraction-limited condition is achieved according to the Maréchal criterion [Smith, 2008]) at a distance up to ~165 µm from the optical axis with the corrective lens, while only up to ~70 µm for the same optical system without the corrective lens (Figure 2a).
evidence: The text explicitly states the Strehl ratio performance without the corrective lens, referencing Figure 2a.

claim: Type I eFOV-microendoscopes showed a ~5 times increase in the area of the diffraction-limited FOV compared to uncorrected probes.
source: This improvement led to a ~5 times increase in the area of the diffraction-limited FOV.
evidence: The text explicitly states the fold increase in diffraction-limited FOV area for type I microendoscopes.

claim: The area of the FOV was ~2–9 times larger for type II-IV eFOV-microendoscopes compared to microendoscopes without the corrective lens.
source: Simulations showed that the area of the FOV was ~2–9 times larger for these other types of eFOV-microendoscopes, compared to microendoscopes without the corrective lens.
evidence: The text explicitly states the range of FOV area increase for types II-IV microendoscopes.

claim: The axial dimension of the PSF in lateral portions of the FOV remained smaller and more similar to the axial dimension of the PSF in the center of the FOV in corrected compared to uncorrected endoscopes.
source: We found that the axial dimension of the PSF in lateral portions of the FOV remained smaller and more similar to the axial dimension of the PSF in the center of the FOV in corrected compared to uncorrected endoscopes.
evidence: The text explicitly states the comparison of axial PSF dimensions between corrected and uncorrected endoscopes, referencing Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2.

source: Fabricated lenses had profile largely overlapping with the simulated one (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).

claim: eFOV-microendoscopes had similar on-axis axial resolution compared to uncorrected probes.
source: We found that eFOV-microendoscopes had similar on-axis axial resolution compared to uncorrected probes (Figure 3c,e,g,i left and Supplementary file 1 - Table 3).
evidence: The text explicitly states the comparison of on-axis axial resolution, with reference to figures and a supplementary table.

source: As expected by ray-trace simulations (Figure 2), eFOV-microendoscopes displayed higher and more homogeneous axial resolution in a larger portion of the FOV (Figure 3c,e,g,i left and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The text explicitly states the improved axial resolution across the FOV, with references to multiple figures.

claim: Corrected microendoscopes had ~3.2–9.4 folds larger effective FOV compared to uncorrected probes when defining effective FOV as that in which FWHMz <10 µm.
source: Defining the effective FOV as that in which FWHMz <10 µm (dotted line in Figure 3c,e,g,i left), we found ~3.2–9.4 folds larger effective FOV in corrected microendoscopes compared to uncorrected probes (Supplementary file 1 - Table 3).
evidence: The text explicitly states the fold increase in effective FOV with a specific definition, referencing figures and a supplementary table.

claim: The small cross-section of the eFOV-microendoscopes preserved thalamocortical and corticothalamic connectivity.
source: We first showed that the small cross-section of the eFOV-microendoscopes developed here preserved thalamocortical and corticothalamic connectivity (Figure 5), a fundamental prerequisite for VPM physiology and a hardly achievable task with larger cross-section GRIN lenses or with chronic windows (Figure 3—figure supplement 7e).
evidence: The text explicitly states that connectivity was preserved, with reference to Figure 5 showing the experimental evidence.

claim: There was no difference in the percentage of pixels displaying green and red signals in implanted vs. non-implanted mice.
source: Importantly, we found no difference in the percentage of pixels displaying green and red signals in implanted vs. non-implanted mice (Figure 5f).
evidence: The text explicitly states the finding of no difference, with reference to Figure 5f showing the quantification.

claim: Active periods displayed an increase in both frequency and amplitude of calcium signals across VPM neurons compared to Q periods.
source: In contrast, active periods displayed an increase in both frequency and amplitude of calcium signals across VPM neurons compared to Q periods (average frequency: fQ = 1.95 ± 0.02 Hz, fA = 2.22 ± 0.02 Hz, Student's t-test p=2E-74, n = 24 t-series from four mice; average amplitude: AQ = 0.137 ± 0.005 ΔF/F0, AA = 0.245 ± 0.008 ΔF/F0, Student's t -test p=2E-128, n = 24 t-series from four mice).
evidence: The text explicitly states the increase in frequency and amplitude with specific values and statistical tests.

claim: Using corrected probes allowed to segment more ROIs with high SNR, shifting the distribution of SNR across ROIs to higher mean SNR values.
source: Rather, the use of corrected probes allowed to segment more ROIs with high SNR, shifting the distribution of SNR across ROIs to higher mean SNR values (Figure 4d, p=1E-5 for ANOVA with respect to the interaction, and Figure 4e).
evidence: The text explicitly states the effect of corrected probes on SNR distribution, with statistical test results and figure references.

claim: ROIs segmented from eFOV-microendoscopes displayed larger correlation with the ground truth signal of an individual neuron compared to uncorrected probes.
source: We found that ROIs segmented from eFOV-microendoscopes displayed larger correlation with the ground truth signal of an individual neuron (Figure 4h left) and lower correlation with the ground truth signal of other nearby neurons (Figure 4h right) compared to uncorrected probes, suggesting that aberration correction allowed to collect more precisely from single cellular emitters and with decreased cross-contamination between neurons.
evidence: The text explicitly states the finding of larger correlation with ground truth in corrected probes, with figure references.

claim: The linear fit of pairwise correlations as a function of radial distance for uncorrected endoscopes had a significantly positive slope.
source: Moreover, the linear fit of pairwise correlations as a function of radial distance for uncorrected endoscopes had a significantly positive slope (Figure 4m, left panel), indicating higher pairwise correlations in lateral compared to more central portions of the FOV.
evidence: The text explicitly states the finding of a positive slope for uncorrected endoscopes, with figure reference and interpretation.

source: For corrected endoscopes, the slope of the linear fit was not significantly different from zero (Figure 4m, right panel), in agreement with the analysis of the artificial calcium t-series (Figure 4g).
evidence: The text explicitly states the finding of no significant slope for corrected endoscopes, with figure references.

source: We found that many neurons were informative about whisking, but only a fraction were particularly informative (Figure 7b).

source: Information of single cells correlated positively with the SNR of their calcium signals (Figure 7f), with higher amount of information carried, on average, by cells displaying higher SNR (Figure 7g).
evidence: The text explicitly states the positive correlation between information and SNR, with figure references.

claim: The large majority of modules was positively modulated by whisking (WMI >0 for 89.6 ± 0.4% of total modules number).
source: We computed the whisking modulation index (WMI, see Materials and methods for definition) and found that the large majority of modules was positively modulated by whisking (WMI >0 for 89.6 ± 0.4% of total modules number, n = 24 FOVs), while the activity of a minority of modules was suppressed during whisking periods (negatively modulated, WMI <0 for 10.4 ± 0.4% of total modules number, n = 24 FOVs).
evidence: The text explicitly states the percentage of positively modulated modules with specific values.

claim: The activity of a minority of modules was suppressed during whisking periods (negatively modulated, WMI <0 for 10.4 ± 0.4% of total modules number).
source: We computed the whisking modulation index (WMI, see Materials and methods for definition) and found that the large majority of modules was positively modulated by whisking (WMI >0 for 89.6 ± 0.4% of total modules number, n = 24 FOVs), while the activity of a minority of modules was suppressed during whisking periods (negatively modulated, WMI <0 for 10.4 ± 0.4% of total modules number, n = 24 FOVs).
evidence: The text explicitly states the percentage of negatively modulated modules with specific values.

source: Sparseness of modules appeared to be negatively correlated with the WMI, suggesting that those few modules that were negatively modulated by whisking were also characterized by few, but highly-informative neurons (within the ensemble) (Figure 7k).
